p: Luke pairs dynamis, power, with exousia, the right to use it. Mark speaks only of authority.
b: Mark 6:7 says Jesus gave the Twelve exousia, authority, over unclean spirits. Luke adds dynamis, power, the word he uses for the Spirit's power at work in Jesus (4:14; 4:36; 5:17) and promised to the church (24:49; Acts 1:8). The Twelve now share the same power and authority that astonished the synagogue at Capernaum (4:36), over demons and over disease alike. In Luke this first mission is a small model of Acts, where the apostles heal and announce the kingdom in Jesus' name.

a: to announce the kingdom of God and to heal the sick
p: The Twelve are sent to do exactly what Jesus has been doing. Acts ends with Paul still doing it.
b: Jesus said he was sent to tell the good news of the kingdom of God to the towns (4:43), and Luke has just shown him doing it, with the Twelve beside him (8:1). Now they are sent to do the same: announce the kingdom and heal. The pairing of word and healing runs through Luke-Acts (9:11; 10:9; Acts 4:30; Acts 8:6–7), and the last verse of Acts shows Paul in Rome still "proclaiming the kingdom of God" (Acts 28:31), where Luke uses the same verb. Luke's readers could see their own mission begin here.

p: Mark lets them take a staff and sandals; Matthew and Luke forbid the staff. Readers have long tried to explain the difference.
b: In Mark 6:8–9 the Twelve may carry a staff and wear sandals. Matthew 10:10 forbids both, and Luke here forbids the staff (and in 10:4 the sandals). Old harmonizers said Matthew forbids getting a new staff (his verb is "acquire") while Mark allows the one you have; Augustine thought "staff" meant two different things. Most scholars think Matthew and Luke had a second, stricter form of the charge from the sayings source they share (often called Q), which Luke also uses for the seventy-two (10:4). Either way the point is the same: go light and depend on God and on the people who take you in. Luke later has Jesus recall this charge and change it for a harder time (22:35–36).

a: shake your feet free of its dust
p: A public sign of breaking off: the town has refused God's messengers, and the messengers leave it to God.
b: Travelers shook off road dust anyway; done on purpose at the town gate, it said, "We take nothing of yours with us, not even your dust." Luke sharpens Mark's "as evidence to them" (Mark 6:11) into "as evidence against them": the act will stand as testimony on the day of judgment (10:12). Paul and Barnabas do exactly this when they are driven out of Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51), and Paul shakes out his clothes at Corinth (Acts 18:6). The sign is a warning, not a curse; the messengers do not call down punishment (compare 9:54–55).

p: Luke, like Matthew, gives Antipas his correct title. Mark calls him king.
b: This is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. Rome never let him use the title king; he was a tetrarch, "ruler of a fourth" of his father's realm (3:1). Mark 6:14 calls him "King Herod," as people loosely did; Matthew 14:1 and Luke use the exact title. Antipas plays a larger part in Luke than in any other Gospel: he imprisons John (3:19–20), wants to see Jesus (9:9), wants to kill him (13:31), and finally meets him at the trial (23:6–12).

t: Luke does not tell how John died
p: Luke leaves out Mark's long story of Herodias' daughter and the banquet. Josephus gives a political reason for the killing.
b: Mark 6:17–29 tells the story of John's death at Herod's birthday banquet. Luke mentions only that Herod locked John up (3:19–20); here, in Herod's own words, the reader learns that John is dead. Josephus also reports the execution, at the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea, and gives Herod's motive as fear that John's influence over the crowds would lead to revolt (Antiquities 18.116–119). The two accounts can stand together: a ruler could fear both a prophet's rebuke and his following.

a: he kept looking for a chance to see him
p: A thread Luke picks up at the trial, where Herod finally gets his wish and is disappointed.
b: Herod's curiosity is not faith. Luke's Pharisees later warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill him (13:31), and when Pilate sends Jesus to Herod during the trial, Luke says Herod was very glad, because he had long wanted to see him and hoped to see a sign (23:8). Jesus gives him not a word (23:9). Seeing Jesus, in Luke, is not the same as seeing who he is (10:23–24).

p: "House of fishing," at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. Two sites are claimed for it, and its place in this story is puzzling.
b: Bethsaida lay near where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee, just outside Antipas' territory, in the lands of Herod's son Philip. Josephus says Philip raised it to the rank of a city and named it Julias after the emperor's daughter (Antiquities 18.28). It was the home of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Archaeologists dispute its site: et-Tell, excavated since 1987, or el-Araj, nearer the old shoreline, excavated since 2016. Luke sets the feeding near Bethsaida, while Mark has the disciples sail toward Bethsaida after it (Mark 6:45); Luke leaves out the Markan section where that happens (see the note on 9:18). Bethsaida is one of the towns Jesus later grieves over (10:13).

p: Apodechomai, to welcome gladly. Mark's Jesus wanted rest; Luke's Jesus welcomes the crowd that interrupts it.
b: In Mark 6:31 Jesus takes the apostles away to rest, and his heart goes out to the crowd that follows. Luke says he "welcomed" them, a word for receiving guests gladly. Luke uses it of the believers who welcomed Peter's message (Acts 2:41) and, in the last scene of Acts, of Paul in Rome: "He welcomed everyone who came in to see him" (Acts 28:30). Before he feeds anyone, Jesus is already the host, and the meal that follows completes the welcome.

p: Feeding a crowd in a deserted place recalls the manna and Elisha's twenty loaves.
b: The Greek erēmos is the word for wilderness. Israel was fed with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16; Psalm 78:24–25), and Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, "and there was extra" (2 Kings 4:44). Luke's story echoes both: a prophet like Elijah and Elisha (9:8, 19), and more than a prophet, feeds God's people in a desert place, with food left over.

p: Mark has hundreds and fifties. Israel in the wilderness was organized into groups of fifty, and so was the Qumran community.
b: Mark 6:40 has the people reclining "in hundreds and in fifties"; Luke keeps only the fifties. Moses set leaders over the people "as captains of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens" (Exodus 18:21), and the community of the Dead Sea Scrolls arranged itself in the same way when it gathered (the Community Rule, 1QS 2:21–22). Some scholars see a hint of the new Israel of the end time gathered for a meal; others think the detail simply makes the scene orderly. The dining groups (klisiai) are groups reclining at a meal, as at a banquet.

p: Luke alone says Jesus blessed the loaves themselves. The four actions return at the Last Supper and at Emmaus.
b: A Jewish meal began with a blessing of God over the bread: "Blessed are you ... who brings forth bread from the earth" (Mishnah Berakhot 6:1). Mark 6:41 says Jesus "said the blessing"; Luke writes that he blessed them, the loaves and fish. The sequence of took, blessed, broke and gave comes again at the Last Supper (22:19) and when the risen Jesus is recognized "in the breaking of the bread" at Emmaus (24:30–35). Many readers, ancient and modern, hear the church's Lord's Supper behind the feeding; others think Luke means no more than a host's grace before a meal.

p: One basket for each of the Twelve who had doubted there was enough.
b: The leftovers fill twelve baskets, the number of Israel's tribes and of the apostles who had just said they had only five loaves (9:13). The kophinos was a sturdy basket of the kind Roman writers mocked as a sign of Jewish travelers (Juvenal, Satires 3.14). Luke tells only this one feeding; the feeding of four thousand with its seven baskets falls in the part of Mark he leaves out (see the next note).

p: Between 9:17 and 9:18 Luke skips Mark 6:45–8:26, a long block of stories. Scholars have offered several reasons.
b: Luke follows Mark closely through the feeding of the five thousand (Mark 6:44) and then picks him up again at Peter's confession (Mark 8:27). Everything between is missing: the walking on the sea, the dispute about washed hands, the Syrophoenician woman, the deaf man, the four thousand, the blind man at Bethsaida. Explanations include: Luke's copy of Mark lacked the section; Luke avoided doublets (a second feeding, a second sea crossing); he saved the question of Gentiles and food laws for Acts 10–15; or he needed the space on his scroll for his own material in 9:51–18:14. The result is that Herod's question "Who is this?" (9:9) is answered almost at once by Peter (9:20).

p: Luke places Jesus at prayer before the turning points of his story. Here it is the question that leads to Peter's confession.
b: Mark sets the scene on the road to Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27); Luke drops the place and puts Jesus at prayer instead. He does this at every turn: at his baptism (3:21), before choosing the Twelve (6:12), here, on the mountain (9:28–29), before teaching the Lord's Prayer (11:1), on the Mount of Olives (22:41–44) and on the cross (23:46, and 23:34 in many manuscripts). Luke's readers learn that what Jesus says and does flows from his life with the Father.

p: Luke's form of the confession. Mark has "the Messiah," Matthew adds "the Son of the living God."
b: Peter's answer in Luke is ton christon tou theou, "the Messiah of God," the anointed king God has chosen. Luke uses the same form at the cross, where the rulers sneer at him as God's Messiah and Chosen One (23:35), and Simeon was promised he would see "the Lord's Messiah" (2:26). The phrase echoes Psalm 2:2 and 1 Samuel's "the LORD's anointed." Luke also leaves out what follows in Matthew and Mark: Jesus' blessing of Peter (Matthew 16:17–19) and Peter's rebuke of Jesus, with "Get behind me, Satan" (Mark 8:32–33). Some see Luke sparing Peter; others think he simply moves straight to the teaching on suffering.
orig: τὸν χριστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ (ton christon tou theou)

a: ordered them to say this to no one
p: Jesus forbids them to spread the title Messiah. In Luke the reason follows at once: the Messiah must suffer.
b: All three Gospels have the order to silence. Luke joins it straight to the prediction of suffering (9:22 is one sentence with 9:21 in the Greek), which suggests the reason: "Messiah" meant a conquering king to most hearers, and Jesus would not take that title until he could show what kind of Messiah he was, one who suffers and is raised. Some scholars see here the "messianic secret" that William Wrede found in Mark (see the topic on Mark); others think the silence simply reflects the danger of the title under Herod and Rome.

p: Dei, "it is necessary." Luke uses it again and again for what God's plan requires.
b: The little Greek verb dei, "it must, it has to," carries one of Luke's main themes. Jesus "had to" be in his Father's house (2:49), "has to" tell the good news to other towns (4:43), "has to" go on to Jerusalem (13:33), and the Son of Man "has to" suffer (17:25; 24:7). On Easter day the risen Jesus asks whether the Messiah did not have to suffer these things (24:26) and explains that everything written about him had to be fulfilled (24:44). The suffering is not an accident or a defeat; it is the path God laid down in the Scriptures.

a: pick up his cross every day
p: Only Luke adds "every day." Taking up the cross becomes a way of life, not only a readiness to die.
b: In Mark 8:34 and Matthew 16:24 the saying pictures a condemned man carrying his crossbeam to execution: follow me even to death. Luke adds kath' hēmeran, "every day." Many interpreters, such as Fitzmyer, take this to mean that Luke applies a martyrs' saying to the daily life of Christians in a time without constant persecution. Others hold that the literal sense stays: each day the disciple must be ready to die, as Paul says he dies every day (1 Corinthians 15:31). Most Byzantine manuscripts lack "every day" (see the variant), but the KJV has "daily."

p: Galileans knew what it meant. Rome made the condemned carry the crossbeam to the place of death.
b: A person sentenced to crucifixion was usually made to carry the crossbeam through the streets to the place of execution, as Simon of Cyrene carried it for Jesus (23:26). Galileans had seen it: after a revolt in 4 BC the Roman governor Varus crucified two thousand men near Jerusalem (Josephus, Jewish War 2.75). Jesus says this before his own death, so the first hearers would have heard it as a stark picture of walking to execution, not yet as a picture of his cross in particular.

a: if he loses himself, or pays for it with himself
p: Where Mark says "his life" (psychē), Luke writes "himself." He explains the Semitic idea for Greek readers.
b: In 9:24 the word for "life" is psychē, which can mean life, soul or self. Mark 8:36 says the person who wins the world "pays for it with his life" (psychē). Luke writes "himself" (heauton) instead, which makes plain that the saying is about losing one's very self, not only one's physical life. He keeps the same verb, apollymi, from 9:24: whoever would save his life will lose it, and the one who wins the world loses himself. The second verb, zēmioō, is a business word: to suffer a loss, to be fined. The whole world is a poor trade for yourself.
orig: ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἀπολέσας ἢ ζημιωθείς (heauton de apolesas ē zēmiōtheis)

a: in his own glory, and his Father's, and the holy angels'
p: Luke speaks of the Son of Man's own glory, as well as the Father's and the angels'.
b: Mark 8:38 has the Son of Man coming "in the glory of his Father, along with the holy angels." Luke speaks of three glories, beginning with "his own." The picture rests on Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives glory and a kingdom. The disciples are about to see a glimpse of that glory on the mountain (9:32). Luke also drops Mark's "in this adulterous and sinful generation," perhaps because his Gentile readers would not hear it as Jesus' Jewish hearers did.

p: Luke often replaces Jesus' Hebrew "Amen" with the Greek word for "truly."
b: Mark 9:1 begins this saying with "Amen, I tell you," Jesus' own way of opening a solemn statement. Luke keeps "Amen" only six times (4:24; 12:37; 18:17; 18:29; 21:32; 23:43) and elsewhere uses the Greek alēthōs, "truly" (here; 12:44; 21:3), or simply "I tell you." He also never uses the word "Rabbi" (see the note on 9:33). For a reader like Theophilus the Greek words were clearer.

a: before they see the kingdom of God
p: Luke drops Mark's "arrived in power." Readers disagree about what some of the bystanders were to see before they died.
b: Mark 9:1 says some will see "the kingdom of God arrived in power"; Matthew 16:28, "the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." Luke says only that they will "see the kingdom of God." Readings: (1) the transfiguration that follows at once, where three of them see Jesus' glory (most church fathers; Luke's arrangement supports it); (2) the resurrection, ascension and the coming of the Spirit (Acts 1–2), when the kingdom comes in power; (3) the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (preterist readers); (4) the kingdom already present in Jesus' works (11:20; 17:21). Hans Conzelmann argued that Luke softened Mark's wording because the end had not come as soon as the first Christians expected; others reply that Luke still expects it (21:32).

p: Mark and Matthew say "six days later." Luke says "about eight days," perhaps counting inclusively, perhaps for a reason.
b: The simplest explanation is a different way of counting: a week counted from one Sunday to the next is "eight days" in Greek and Jewish reckoning (John 20:26). Luke's "about" also shows he is not stressing the number. Some see a deliberate sign: early Christians called Sunday, the day of the resurrection, "the eighth day" (Epistle of Barnabas 15:9), and the Feast of Booths lasted eight days (Leviticus 23:36), which may fit Peter's three booths (9:33).

a: his face took on a different look
p: Mark and Matthew say Jesus was "transformed" (metamorphoō). Luke says only that his face looked different.
b: Luke does not use metamorphoō, the verb behind "metamorphosis" and "transfiguration" (Mark 9:2; Matthew 17:2). Many scholars think Gentile readers might have heard in it the shape-changing gods of Greek myth, the subject of Ovid's Metamorphoses. Luke speaks instead of the appearance of his face, which recalls Moses: "the skin of his face was shining from his speaking with him" (Exodus 34:29). The shining in Luke comes while Jesus is praying.
orig: τὸ εἶδος τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ ἕτερον (to eidos tou prosōpou autou heteron)

p: Luke's verb comes from the word for lightning. The same image returns at Satan's fall, the Son of Man's day and the empty tomb.
b: Exastraptō, "flash like lightning," is built on astrapē, lightning. Luke uses the image for heaven breaking in: Satan falling "like lightning out of heaven" (10:18), the day of the Son of Man that lights up the sky like lightning (17:24), and the two men at the tomb in clothes that flashed like lightning (24:4). Daniel's heavenly man has a face "like lightning" (Daniel 10:6).

t: Two men at three turning points
p: "And look, two men": Luke uses the same words at the transfiguration, the empty tomb and the ascension.
b: Luke calls Moses and Elijah "two men" before naming them. The same phrase introduces the two figures in shining clothes at the empty tomb (24:4) and the "two men in white clothing" at the ascension (Acts 1:10). The three scenes are tied together: here they speak of his exodus to be completed in Jerusalem (9:31); at the tomb they announce it done; at the ascension they promise his return. Some readers think Luke means Moses and Elijah in all three; most think he simply links the scenes.

p: The Greek word is exodos. It means a departure, and here also death, and it points to Israel's way out of Egypt.
b: Luke alone says what the three men talked about: Jesus' exodos, which he was about to "complete" or "fulfill" in Jerusalem. The word can mean death, as when 2 Peter 1:15 speaks of Peter's "exodus" and Wisdom of Solomon 3:2–3 of the righteous whose "going" was thought an affliction and their leaving a disaster. But with Moses standing there, readers would think of the exodus from Egypt. Many scholars read Luke's whole story from here to Jerusalem as a new exodus: Jesus leads God's people out of a deeper slavery through his death, resurrection and ascension, as the prophet like Moses (9:35; Deuteronomy 18:15). David Moessner traced how the travel narrative follows Moses' journey in Deuteronomy.

p: Only Luke says the three were heavy with sleep. They will sleep again on the Mount of Olives.
b: The detail suggests the scene happened at night, as prayer often did (6:12). It also prepares for Gethsemane, where Luke says Jesus found the disciples asleep from grief (22:45). Daniel falls into a deep sleep when the heavenly messenger speaks (Daniel 8:18; Daniel 10:9). The verb diagrēgoreō can mean that they kept awake through their drowsiness or that they came fully awake; on the second reading they had fallen asleep and woke to the glory. Either way Luke's point holds: they nearly missed it, but they saw his glory, as the apostles later claimed to be eyewitnesses of it (2 Peter 1:16–18; John 1:14).

p: Mark has Peter say "Rabbi." Luke, who never uses the Hebrew word, has epistata, a Greek title for someone in charge.
b: Epistatēs means an overseer, someone set over others. Only Luke uses it of Jesus, always from disciples or from people asking his help (5:5; 8:24; 8:45; 9:33; 9:49; 17:13). Where Mark has "Rabbi" (Mark 9:5) or "Teacher" (Mark 9:38), Luke gives a Greek word his readers would understand. It is a title of respect for a leader, not yet the full confession "Lord."

p: The same verb describes the Spirit coming on Mary (1:35) and the cloud of God's presence on the tent in the wilderness.
b: Episkiazō, "to overshadow," is the verb of 1:35, where the Most High's power "will cast its shadow over you." In the Greek Old Testament it describes the cloud that settled on the tent of meeting, so that Moses could not enter while the glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35). The disciples enter the cloud, a sign of God's own presence, as Moses went into the cloud on Sinai (Exodus 24:18). Their fear is the right response to it.

p: The voice repeats Moses' words about the prophet God would raise up.
b: Moses promised, "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me ... You must listen to him" (Deuteronomy 18:15). Peter's sermon applies the promise to Jesus (Acts 3:22–23), and so does Stephen's (Acts 7:37). On the mountain, with Moses standing by, God points to Jesus as that prophet. What they must listen to is what Jesus has just said: that the Son of Man must suffer (9:22–26). The first half of the saying joins Psalm 2:7 ("my Son") and Isaiah 42:1 ("my chosen one").

a: In those days they did not report
t: No order of silence, no talk of Elijah
p: In Mark, Jesus orders silence on the way down and discusses Elijah. Luke leaves both out: the disciples simply say nothing.
b: Mark 9:9–13 has Jesus forbid the three to tell anyone until the Son of Man rises, followed by the question about Elijah coming first and Jesus' answer that Elijah has come (John the Baptist). Luke has neither. The disciples keep silent of their own accord, "in those days," which implies they spoke later (2 Peter 1:16–18). Luke may have left out the Elijah discussion because he had already said John would come "with Elijah's spirit and power" (1:17) and because, in his Gospel, Jesus himself is often compared with Elijah (4:25–26; 7:11–17; 9:54).

a: He is the only child I have
p: Only Luke says the boy was an only child, as he does for the widow's son and Jairus' daughter.
b: Monogenēs means "only" (of a son or daughter). Luke adds it three times in healing stories: the widow of Nain's only son (7:12), Jairus' only daughter (8:42) and this boy. Each time a parent stands to lose everything. In John the same word describes Jesus as the Father's "only Son" (John 3:16). Luke shows Jesus giving back to parents the one child they had, as Elijah gave back the widow's son (1 Kings 17:23; 9:42).

a: a spirit takes hold of him
p: The symptoms sound like epileptic seizures. The Gospel names a spirit; the ancient world argued about such illnesses too.
b: Screaming, falling, convulsions and foaming at the mouth match what doctors now call epileptic seizures, and Matthew 17:15 calls the boy "moonstruck," the ancient name for the illness. Greek doctors had already argued that the "sacred disease" had natural causes (Hippocratic writing On the Sacred Disease). Luke calls it a spirit and a demon (9:42). Some Christians read the story as healing an illness described in the language of its time; others hold that a spirit really caused it; many say both can be true. Luke's account is shorter than Mark's, leaving out the father's "Help me with my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24). The old claim that Luke's medical vocabulary proves he was a physician (Hobart, 1882) was answered by Henry Cadbury, who showed that other Greek writers used the same words.

p: Jesus' words echo Moses' song about Israel in the wilderness.
b: The Song of Moses calls Israel "a warped and twisted generation" (Deuteronomy 32:5), and Paul echoes the same verse for the world around the church (Philippians 2:15). Coming down from the mountain to find failure below, Jesus speaks like Moses coming down Sinai to the golden calf (Exodus 32). The rebuke takes in the whole generation, the crowd and the disciples who could not help the boy (9:40).

p: Megaleiotēs, majesty. In Luke the crowd sees God's greatness in Jesus' deed; 2 Peter uses the word for the transfiguration.
b: Luke often ends a healing with praise to God (5:25–26; 7:16; 13:13; 17:15; 18:43). Here the people are stunned at the "grandeur" or "majesty" of God. The rare word megaleiotēs appears in 2 Peter 1:16, where the apostles say they were eyewitnesses of his majesty on the holy mountain, and in Acts 19:27 of the goddess Artemis. Luke lets the reader see that the power at work in Jesus is God's own.

p: Paradidōmi: to hand over, betray, deliver. The Son of Man is handed over to men, a play on words in Aramaic.
b: The verb is used for Judas betraying Jesus (22:4, 6, 21), for the council handing him to Pilate (20:20; 24:20) and for God giving him up (Romans 8:32). In this second prediction Luke keeps only the handing over, not the killing and rising (compare 9:22). Joachim Jeremias noted a play on words that works in Aramaic: bar enasha, "son of man," handed over to bene enasha, "sons of men." The one who is truly human is given into the hands of humans.
orig: παραδίδοσθαι εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώπων (paradidosthai eis cheiras anthrōpōn)

a: It had been covered over from them
p: The passive suggests God hid the meaning for now. Understanding comes only after Easter.
b: Luke says the saying was "covered over" (parakekalymmenon) from the disciples "so that" they could not perceive it. Many read this as God's own hiding, a divine passive, like the eyes of the Emmaus pair that were "kept from" recognizing Jesus (24:16). Others see the disciples' own resistance, or the work of Satan (22:3, 31). Luke repeats the point after the third prediction (18:34). Only the risen Jesus, opening their minds to the Scriptures, makes them understand (24:25–27, 45).

a: which of them would rank highest
p: The disciples argue about rank right after a prediction of his death, and they will do it again at the Last Supper.
b: In Luke the same quarrel breaks out at the table on the night before Jesus dies (22:24). Both times Jesus answers by turning the order of rank upside down (9:48; 22:26–27). In a society built on honor and seating order, the question was natural; Jesus' answer was not.

p: Children had no status. To welcome a child for Jesus' sake is to welcome Jesus, and God who sent him.
b: In the Greek and Roman world, and in Judea too, a child was a minor with no rights, valued for what he would become. Jesus stands a child beside himself, the place of honor, and makes the child his representative: to take in this child is to take him in. The principle of the messenger who stands for the sender appears again when he sends out the seventy-two (10:16). Luke's lesson for the church: greatness is measured by who you are willing to serve and receive.

a: throwing out demons in your name
t: An outsider who uses the name
p: John wants to stop him. Moses faced the same complaint about Eldad and Medad, and Acts shows people misusing the name.
b: When two men prophesied in the camp without coming to the tent, Joshua asked Moses to stop them, and Moses answered, "If only all the LORD's people were prophets" (Numbers 11:29). Jesus answers John in the same spirit. Acts shows the other side: Jewish exorcists at Ephesus who said, "I put you under oath by Jesus, the one Paul preaches!" (Acts 19:13), using the name as a formula, and were overpowered by the spirit (Acts 19:13–16). The difference lies in whether the name is used in faith. This John is the John who will soon ask to call down fire (9:54).

t: Not against you, or not with me?
p: Here Jesus says whoever is not against you is for you. In 11:23 he says whoever is not with him is against him.
b: The two sayings seem to clash: "Anyone who is not against you is on your side" (here) and "Anyone who is not on my side is against me" (Matthew 12:30; compare Luke 11:23). Most interpreters see two different situations. Here the question is how disciples treat someone outside their group who is doing good in Jesus' name: be generous. In 11:23 the question is how a person stands toward Jesus himself, in the conflict with Satan: no one can be neutral. The church has used the first saying to urge tolerance of other Christians and the second to urge decision.

p: Analēmpsis: a taking up. Luke uses the verb for Jesus' ascension, as the Greek Bible did for Elijah's.
b: The noun analēmpsis appears only here in the New Testament. Its verb analambanō is Luke's word for the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11, 22) and the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Elijah being taken up in the windstorm (2 Kings 2:9–11; Sirach 48:9). Some interpreters take "taken up" to mean Jesus' death, as the word sometimes meant in Greek; most think Luke has in view the whole movement of death, resurrection and ascension to God. Either way the journey ahead does not end at the cross.

p: A Hebrew way of saying firm resolve. The Servant in Isaiah set his face like flint; Ezekiel was told to set his face against Jerusalem.
b: The phrase is an idiom from the Greek Old Testament. The Servant of the LORD, facing insult and beating, says, "I have made my face hard as flint" (Isaiah 50:7). God tells Ezekiel to set his face toward Jerusalem and prophesy against it (Ezekiel 21:2). Both senses fit: Jesus goes knowing he will suffer, and he goes as a prophet to a city that kills prophets (13:33–34). This verse opens the long journey section of Luke, about ten chapters, which ends when he reaches Jerusalem (19:41–44).

a: He sent messengers before his face
p: The words recall Malachi's messenger, which Luke used for John the Baptist (7:27). Now Jesus sends his own.
b: Jesus applied Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1 to John: "Look, I am sending my messenger before your face" (7:27). Here Jesus himself sends messengers (angelous, the word also used for angels) "before his face," and in 10:1 he sends the seventy-two the same way. The prophet who prepared his way is gone (9:9); now his own followers prepare his way.

p: The quickest road from Galilee to Jerusalem ran through Samaria, and Samaritans and Jews were bitter rivals.
b: The Samaritans worshiped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses, but on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem (John 4:20). The Judean ruler John Hyrcanus had destroyed their temple there around 110 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.255–256). Josephus says Galileans going up to the festivals usually passed through Samaria, a three-day journey (Life 269), and he reports that in about AD 52 Samaritans of the village of Ginae killed Galilean pilgrims, which set off armed clashes (Antiquities 20.118–136 speaks of many killed; Jewish War 2.232 of one Galilean). Matthew's Jesus had forbidden the Twelve to enter Samaritan towns (Matthew 10:5); Luke's Jesus tries to stay in one, and Samaritans will soon be the heroes of his stories (10:33; 17:16), as Samaria will be the first mission field beyond Judea in Acts 8.

p: A Hebrew idiom kept in the Greek. The villagers saw that his goal was the temple in Jerusalem, not their holy mountain.
b: The Hebrew Bible can say someone's "face" goes where the person goes (2 Samuel 17:11, literally "your face going into battle"). Luke keeps the image to tie this verse to 9:51 and 9:52: Jesus' face is set on Jerusalem. The Samaritans refuse him because he is a pilgrim to the rival temple; as John explains, "Jews do not share vessels with Samaritans" (John 4:9). This is the first welcome refused on the journey, and Jesus answers it without revenge.
orig: τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἦν πορευόμενον (to prosōpon autou ēn poreuomenon)

a: order fire to come down out of the sky
p: James and John want to do what Elijah did to the king's soldiers. Jesus refuses.
b: When King Ahaziah sent soldiers to arrest him, Elijah said, "If I am a man of God, then let fire come down out of the sky and devour you and your fifty" (2 Kings 1:10). That happened in Samaria. James and John, whom Jesus named "Sons of Thunder" (Mark 3:17), offer to do the same to this Samaritan village. Luke has just shown Jesus with Elijah on the mountain, and Jesus will be "taken up" like Elijah (9:51), but he does not repeat Elijah's fire. In Luke the fire Jesus brings is the Holy Spirit (3:16; 12:49; Acts 2:3). Many manuscripts add "as Elijah did" (see the variant).

a: On the road, as they went along
p: Matthew puts two of these sayings before a lake crossing. Luke sets them on the road to Jerusalem and adds a third.
b: Matthew 8:19–22 has a scribe and a disciple come to Jesus before he crosses the lake. Luke places the sayings at the start of the journey to Jerusalem, so that "wherever you go" means following him to the cross, and adds a third man (9:61–62), whose request recalls Elisha. Luke likes the word "road" (hodos); in Acts the movement of Jesus' followers is called "the Way" (Acts 9:2). Luke does not say whether any of the three followed.

p: Animals have homes; the Son of Man does not. Later in Luke, Jesus calls Herod a fox.
b: Jesus has just been refused lodging in a Samaritan village (9:53), so the saying is concrete: on this road he has nowhere to sleep. The only other fox in Luke is Herod Antipas, whom Jesus calls a fox (13:32): the ruler has a home and a palace; the Son of Man does not. The wording matches Matthew 8:20 exactly in the Greek.

a: Let the dead bury their own dead
p: Burying a father was a sacred duty. Jesus' answer shocked his hearers, and readers have explained it in several ways.
b: Honoring a father included burying him (Genesis 50:5; Tobit 4:3), and later Jewish law freed a son whose father lay unburied even from saying the Shema (Mishnah Berakhot 3:1). Readings: (1) the spiritually dead can bury the physically dead, but the kingdom cannot wait; (2) the father was not yet dead, and the man wanted to wait at home until he died; (3) Byron McCane suggested a second burial, the gathering of bones into an ossuary a year after death, so the delay would be long; (4) Martin Hengel saw a prophetic sign, like God forbidding Jeremiah and Ezekiel to mourn (Jeremiah 16:5–7; Ezekiel 24:15–24), showing that the call of the kingdom outranks even the holiest family duty. Luke adds the positive command: "go off and spread the news of the kingdom of God."

a: say goodbye to those back at my house
p: The third man asks what Elisha asked of Elijah. Elijah allowed it; Jesus does not.
b: When Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha, Elisha said, "Please, let me kiss my father and my mother," and Elijah let him go back (1 Kings 19:20). Elisha then sacrificed his oxen, burned his plow gear and followed. Jesus asks more than Elijah did: the call of the kingdom does not wait even for farewells. The man's words also echo the first: "I will follow you ... but first."

a: set his hand on a plow
p: A light plow was steered with one hand. Look behind you, and the furrow goes crooked.
b: The plow of Jesus' day was a wooden frame with an iron tip, guided with one hand while the other drove the oxen with a goad. The plowman had to keep his eyes fixed ahead to cut a straight furrow. Greek writers used the same picture as early as Hesiod, who praised the plowman who keeps his mind on his work and his furrow straight (Works and Days 441–445). The saying ties back to Elisha, who was plowing when Elijah called him (1 Kings 19:19), and forward to Lot's wife, who looked back (17:32).

p: Luke the narrator often calls Jesus simply "the Lord," far more than Mark or Matthew do.
b: From 7:13 on, Luke sometimes calls Jesus "the Lord" in his own storytelling, not only in what characters say (7:19 and 10:39 in some editions; 10:41; 11:39; 12:42; 13:15; 17:5–6; 18:6; 19:8; 22:61; and 24:3, where some manuscripts lack "of the Lord Jesus"). Mark never does this before the Longer Ending, and Matthew rarely. Luke writes after Easter, when Christians confessed "Jesus is Lord" (Acts 2:36; Romans 10:9), and lets that title color the story of his earthly life.

p: The number recalls the nations of Genesis 10 and the elders of Moses. The manuscripts are split between seventy and seventy-two.
b: In the Hebrew text Genesis 10 lists seventy nations descended from Noah's sons; the Greek Septuagint lists seventy-two. So both numbers could stand for the whole world, and many readers see the Gentile mission of Acts foreshadowed: the Twelve stand for Israel's tribes (9:1; 22:30), the seventy-two for the nations. Others point to Moses' seventy elders (Exodus 24:1; Numbers 11:16), to whom later rabbinic tradition added Eldad and Medad to count seventy-two who received the spirit (Numbers 11:24–26; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 17a), though Numbers itself seems to count the two among the seventy, or to the seventy-two elders who translated the Law into Greek in the Letter of Aristeas. Luke does not explain the number. Bruce Metzger's study of the evidence found the two numbers almost evenly supported (see the variant).

a: like lambs into the middle of a pack of wolves
p: Matthew has sheep; Luke has lambs, the most helpless of the flock. The prophets saw wolf and lamb at peace in the age to come.
b: Isaiah pictured the coming age as a time when "The wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb" (Isaiah 11:6; compare Isaiah 65:25). Jesus sends his messengers into a world where that peace has not yet arrived; they go defenseless, carrying only a word of peace (10:5). Paul warns the Ephesian elders of savage wolves who will come in among the flock (Acts 20:29). Matthew 10:16 has "sheep" and adds the advice to be sharp as snakes; Luke has neither.

a: do not greet anybody along the way
p: Not rudeness but urgency. Middle Eastern greetings could take a long time; Elisha gave his servant the same order.
b: A greeting on the road in that world meant blessings, questions about family and often an invitation. Elisha told Gehazi, as he sent him to the dead boy, "Whoever you meet, don't say a blessing to him" (2 Kings 4:29). The messengers are on God's errand and must not be held up. The command does not forbid courtesy; their greeting of peace is kept for the houses they enter (10:5).

p: A Hebrew way of saying a person of peace: someone open to receive the blessing of peace.
b: Hebrew and Aramaic describe a person by the quality that marks him as "son of" it: literally "sons of this age" (16:8; 20:34, where the Plain has "children of this age"), "sons of light" (16:8, "children of light"), "sons of the resurrection" (20:36). A "son of peace" is someone ready to receive the shalom the messengers bring, the peace of God's kingdom that the angels sang at Jesus' birth (2:14) and that Jerusalem did not recognize (19:42). The greeting "Peace" was ordinary, but on their lips it carried power: it either rests on the house or returns to them.

a: a worker has earned his pay
p: Paul's circle quotes this saying with the Law of Moses as Scripture. Matthew's version says "food"; Luke's matches 1 Timothy.
b: 1 Timothy 5:18 gives two sayings as what "the Scripture says": first Deuteronomy 25:4, "Do not muzzle an ox while it is threshing," and then this very saying about the worker and his pay, in exactly Luke's Greek, while Matthew 10:10 has "food" instead of "pay." Some think 1 Timothy treats Luke's Gospel as Scripture; others think both draw on a well-known saying of Jesus. Paul also says the Lord commanded that those who announce the good news should live by it (1 Corinthians 9:14), and the Didache applies the same rule to traveling prophets (Didache 13:1–2).

a: Do not keep changing from one house to another
p: The messengers are not to move around in search of a better host. The early church wrestled with wandering preachers who did.
b: Moving to a richer house would shame the first host and make the mission look like a way to live well. The Didache, a church manual from about AD 100, tells churches to welcome a traveling apostle for a day, or two if needed; one who stays three days, or asks for money, is a false prophet (Didache 11:4–6). Luke's own story shows the pattern of staying put: Peter stays many days with Simon the tanner (Acts 9:43) and Paul with Lydia and with Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 16:15; Acts 18:3).

a: eat what they put in front of you
p: In a Jewish village this meant accepting hospitality without fuss. Some see a hint of the Gentile mission, where food laws would arise.
b: Luke repeats the instruction to eat (10:7, 8). In Galilean and Judean homes, the point is simple: accept what your hosts give and do not insist on your own standards of diet or purity. Paul uses almost the same Greek for Christians eating in Gentile homes: "eat whatever is set before you" without raising questions (1 Corinthians 10:27). Because the seventy-two may stand for the nations (see the note on 10:1), some scholars read the command as preparing for Peter's vision and the debates over food in Acts 10–15. Others warn against reading a later question back into a mission to Jewish towns.

a: the kingdom of God has drawn near.
p: To the town that welcomes them, the kingdom has drawn near "to you" (10:9). To the town that refuses, it has simply drawn near.
b: The message is the same in both towns, but Luke's critical text changes one detail. Where the messengers are welcomed, they say the kingdom has come near "to you" (10:9); where they are refused, they say only that it has come near (the Byzantine text adds "to you" here too). Refusing the messengers does not stop God's reign from arriving; it only means the town has turned away from it. The verb is the same perfect tense used by John and Jesus (Matthew 3:2; Matthew 4:17).

p: Sodom abused God's messengers who came as guests. A town that turns away Jesus' messengers is judged by the same measure.
b: In Genesis 19 the men of Sodom tried to assault the two angels Lot had taken in. Jewish tradition remembered Sodom's sins as pride, plenty and refusal to help the poor (Ezekiel 16:49) and as hostility to strangers (Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–15). The comparison fits a passage about hospitality: Sodom refused God's messengers, but it never heard the message of the kingdom. "On that day" is the day of judgment (10:14; 17:29–30).
r: Genesis 19:1–25; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–15; 17:28–30; Matthew 10:15

p: A Jewish town in the hills above Capernaum, named in the Gospels only in this saying.
b: Chorazin is identified with the ruins of Khirbet Karazeh, about two and a half miles north of Capernaum. The visible remains, including a basalt synagogue, date from a few centuries after Jesus; a carved stone seat found there is often compared with "Moses' seat" (Matthew 23:2). The Gospels record no act of Jesus in Chorazin, a reminder of how much of his work they leave untold (John 21:25). With Bethsaida (9:10) and Capernaum (10:15), it forms a small triangle of towns at the north end of the lake where he did most of his work.

p: The great Phoenician ports, condemned by Israel's prophets, here judged more open than Jesus' own towns.
b: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel and Amos all spoke oracles against Tyre and Sidon for their pride and greed (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28; Amos 1:9–10). Yet Luke has already shown crowds from the region of Tyre and Sidon coming to hear Jesus (6:17), and Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon (4:26). Jesus says these Gentile cities would have repented like Nineveh (11:32; Jonah 3:5–8). The saying is a warning to the towns that saw most and changed least.

p: The words echo Isaiah's taunt over the king of Babylon, who wanted to climb to heaven and was thrown down to Sheol.
b: Isaiah 14 mocks a proud king who said, "I will go up into the heavens" (Isaiah 14:13), and answers, "No! Down to Sheol you are thrust" (Isaiah 14:15). Capernaum, Jesus' base in Galilee (4:31), was lifted high by his presence and his acts of power, but if it does not repent, it will share the tyrant's fall. Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the world of the dead (16:23). The same passage of Isaiah stands behind 10:18.

t: The one sent stands for the sender
p: Jewish law said a man's agent is like the man himself. Jesus' messengers carry his authority, and God's.
b: The Mishnah states a principle older than the rabbis: "a man's agent is like himself" (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5). An agent (shaliach, a word some connect with "apostle") could sign a contract or betroth a bride in his master's name. Jesus applies the rule to his messengers: to hear them is to hear him, to set them aside is to set him aside, and to set him aside is to set aside God who sent him (compare 9:48; Matthew 10:40; John 13:20). How far this authority reaches beyond the first messengers is a question the churches answer differently (see the card on the chapter page).

a: I was watching Satan fall like lightning out of heaven
p: When did Jesus see this? Readers have placed it before creation, at his testing, in the mission itself, or at the end.
b: The Greek joins a past continuous verb ("I was watching") with an aorist participle (pesonta), which after a verb of seeing normally means "watching him fall"; a few take it as "fallen," a state. Readings: (1) a vision in which Jesus saw Satan's defeat, perhaps at his baptism or testing (3:21–22; 4:1–13); (2) a prophetic way of describing what the seventy-two have just done: every demon cast out is Satan's power falling (11:20–22); (3) the fall of Satan before the world began, as many church fathers read it with Isaiah 14:12, "How you have fallen from the heavens, / Shining One, son of Dawn!"; (4) a preview of Satan's final defeat (Revelation 12:7–10; John 12:31). Susan Garrett argues that Luke-Acts tells the story of Satan's overthrow, begun here and finished at the cross and resurrection. Lightning stresses how sudden and visible the fall is (see 9:29).

p: The dangers of Israel's wilderness and the old enemy of Genesis 3 become pictures of the powers of evil.
b: Moses reminded Israel of the wilderness "with its burning snakes and scorpions" (Deuteronomy 8:15), and Psalm 91 promises the one who trusts God, "young lion and serpent you will stamp down" (Psalm 91:13), the psalm Satan quoted to Jesus (4:10–11). Behind it stands the promise that the woman's offspring would strike the serpent on the head (Genesis 3:15). The Testament of Levi, part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs (a work preserved by Christians, with Jewish roots of debated date; this chapter is among those most often thought to have Christian additions), says the coming priest will give his children power to tread on evil spirits (Testament of Levi 18:12). Luke shows the promise kept literally when Paul survives a viper's bite (Acts 28:3–6), but here the main sense is power over "the enemy," Satan.
r: Deuteronomy 8:15; Psalm 91:13; Genesis 3:15; 4:10–11; 11:11–12; Acts 28:3–6; Mark 16:18; Romans 16:20

a: your names stand written in heaven
p: The idea of God's book of the living runs from Moses to Revelation.
b: Moses asked God to wipe him "from your book that you have written" (Exodus 32:32) rather than let Israel perish. The psalmist prays that enemies be "wiped out of the scroll of life" (Psalm 69:28), and Daniel speaks of everyone "found written in the scroll" (Daniel 12:1). The New Testament calls it the book of life (Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12, 15) and the assembly of the firstborn "enrolled in heaven" (Hebrews 12:23). The perfect tense says the names were written and stay written. Joy over power can turn to pride; joy over belonging to God cannot.
r: Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3; Hebrews 12:23; Revelation 20:12

p: Agalliaō: to exult. Only Luke says the Holy Spirit moved Jesus to this prayer, so that Father, Son and Spirit meet in one verse.
b: Agalliaō is the word of Mary's song, where her spirit finds its gladness in God (1:47), and of Psalm 16, which Peter quotes at Pentecost (Acts 2:26). Matthew 11:25 introduces the same prayer with "at that time Jesus spoke up"; Luke says he exulted "in the Holy Spirit," which shows the prayer as Spirit-inspired praise. Church fathers pointed to the verse as a picture of the Trinity: the Son, rejoicing in the Spirit, praising the Father. Joy is one of Luke's great themes, from the angel's news of great joy (2:10) to the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy (24:52).

a: Only the Father knows who the Son is
t: A saying that sounds like John
p: This is the one place in the first three Gospels where Jesus speaks of "the Father" and "the Son" the way John's Gospel does.
b: Nineteenth-century scholars called this saying (with Matthew 11:27) "a thunderbolt from the Johannine sky," because its language of mutual knowing between Father and Son is so close to John (John 3:35; John 10:15; John 17:2). Some critics think the church created it; others, including Joachim Jeremias, defended it as Jesus' own, pointing to Jewish ways of speaking about a father and son who know each other and about Wisdom, known only by God (Job 28:12–27; Sirach 1:6–9; Wisdom of Solomon 9:9–17). Luke's form says "who the Son is" and "who the Father is," a little more like a statement about identity than Matthew's wording.

p: Matthew says "prophets and righteous people." Luke's kings recall David, who foresaw the Messiah.
b: Matthew 13:17 has "many prophets and righteous people wanted badly to see what you are seeing." Luke has "kings," perhaps thinking of David, whom Peter calls a prophet who foresaw the Messiah's resurrection (Acts 2:30–31). 1 Peter 1:10–12 puts the same thought in other words: the prophets searched for the time of the Messiah's sufferings and glory, and angels long to look into it. The blessing falls on those who see Jesus' works and understand them.

a: put a question to him as a test
p: Ekpeirazō is the verb Jesus used when he refused to put God to the test. The lawyer's question is a challenge, not a trap only.
b: Jesus answered the devil, "You must not put the Lord your God to the test" (4:12), using the same verb, ekpeirazō, from Deuteronomy 6:16. A test in Jewish debate was a normal way to measure a teacher's learning (compare Matthew 22:35), and need not be hostile; but Luke's word warns the reader that the lawyer wants to measure Jesus, not to learn. In Mark 12:28–34 the man who asks about the greatest commandment is a friendly scribe whom Jesus praises; Luke tells a different scene, or tells it differently.

p: "Eternal life" is the life of the age to come. A ruler asks the same question in the same words in 18:18.
b: Zōē aiōnios means "life of the age," the life of the coming age that Daniel promised: "some to everlasting life" (Daniel 12:2). "Inherit" is the word for Israel receiving the land (Deuteronomy 4:1). Later rabbis asked who has "a share in the world to come" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). The ruler in 18:18 asks exactly the same question; there Jesus points to the commandments and then asks him to sell everything. Here Jesus lets the lawyer answer from the law himself.

a: with all your heart, with all your being, with all your strength and with all your mind
p: The lawyer joins Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. In Mark and Matthew it is Jesus who does this; Jewish teachers did it too.
b: The first commandment is the Shema: "Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:5). Luke, like Mark 12:30 and Matthew 22:37, adds "mind"; some Greek manuscripts of Deuteronomy already had "mind" for "heart." The second is "You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). In Mark and Matthew Jesus brings the two together; here a Jewish legal expert does it, and Jesus approves. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, preserved by Christians but with Jewish roots of debated date, join love of God and neighbor (Testament of Issachar 5:2; Testament of Dan 5:3), and Philo calls piety toward God and kindness toward people the two chief headings of the law (On the Special Laws 2.63). The pairing was not new; the parable that follows is.
r: Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Leviticus 19:18; Mark 12:29–31; Matthew 22:37–40; Romans 13:9; Galatians 5:14

a: Keep doing this, and you will live
p: Jesus' words echo Leviticus 18:5, a verse Paul later reads in his own way.
b: God told Israel, "If a human being does them, he will live by them" (Leviticus 18:5). Jesus applies it to the two great commandments: keep on doing them, and you will have the life you asked about. Paul quotes Leviticus 18:5 in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12 to contrast the righteousness of the law with the righteousness of faith, because no one keeps the law perfectly. Luke's Jesus speaks without that contrast. How the two fit together is one of the classic debates between the churches (see the card on the chapter page).

p: Dikaioō: here, to show yourself in the right. The lawyer wants a limit on who counts as his neighbor.
b: Having been told to keep doing what he already knew, the lawyer wants to save face and to define his duty. The question "who is my neighbor?" was a real one. In Leviticus 19:18 the neighbor is one of "the children of your people," but Leviticus 19:34 commands Israel to love the foreigner who lives among them "as yourself." Some Jewish groups drew the circle tightly: the Qumran Community Rule taught love for the sons of light and hatred for the sons of darkness (1QS 1:9–10). Jesus will answer by changing the question. On "justify" elsewhere in Luke, see 16:15 and 18:14.

p: About 17 miles, dropping more than 3,000 feet through the Judean desert. It was known for robbers.
b: Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet above sea level and Jericho about 850 feet below it, so the road falls sharply through barren hills. Its steepest part passed the "Ascent of Adummim," the "red" ascent (Joshua 15:7), named for its red rocks; Jerome later wrote that the name meant "of blood" because of the blood robbers shed there (Letter 108). Since the Middle Ages a roadside khan on the route has been shown as "the Inn of the Good Samaritan." Jericho was also a winter resort, with Herod's palaces. Every hearer knew the road and its dangers.

t: Why the priest and Levite passed by
p: Not because the Torah or Judaism required it. Jewish law itself made helping or burying an abandoned man a duty.
b: Some readers have said the priest feared corpse impurity: "A priest must not make himself unclean for a dead person among his kin" (Leviticus 21:1). But the man was not dead, the priest was going down, away from the temple service, and later Jewish law ruled that even a high priest must bury an abandoned body (the met mitzvah, Mishnah Nazir 7:1). Saving a life outweighed almost every other commandment. Amy-Jill Levine notes that Jewish hearers expected a series of "priest, Levite and Israelite," so the shock is not that the clergy failed, but that the third man is a Samaritan. She warns against readings that turn the parable into a picture of cold Judaism or of a Torah that blocked mercy: the story assumes everyone knew the priest and Levite should have stopped.

p: To a Judean hearer, a Samaritan was the last person to expect as the hero. Yet Scripture had a story like this one.
b: Hostility between Jews and Samaritans was centuries old. Sirach calls them "the foolish people that live in Shechem" (Sirach 50:26), and Josephus reports Samaritans scattering human bones in the temple courts at Passover under the governor Coponius, around AD 6–9, to defile it (Antiquities 18.29–30). But 2 Chronicles 28 tells of men of Samaria who clothed, fed and anointed captives from Judah, put the weak on donkeys, and "brought them to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their relatives" (2 Chronicles 28:15). F. Scott Spencer and others think Jesus' story echoes it. The Samaritan has no reason to help a Judean and every reason to fear the same robbers.

a: his heart went out to him
p: Splanchnizomai: the word Luke uses for Jesus at Nain and for the father of the lost son.
b: The verb comes from splanchna, the inner organs, felt as the seat of deep feeling. In Luke it describes Jesus at the sight of the widow at Nain (7:13), the Samaritan here, and the father who runs to his returning son (15:20). In each case pity becomes action. The Samaritan feels what God feels, and does what Jesus does.

a: poured oil and wine on his wounds
p: The usual first aid of the time: wine to clean the wounds, oil to soothe them.
b: Isaiah described Israel as a body with raw wounds that had not been "bandaged / or eased with oil" (Isaiah 1:6). Ancient doctors used wine to clean wounds and oil to soften them. Oil and wine were also offerings poured out in the temple, and Kenneth Bailey noted that the verb for pouring belongs to worship as well, and suggested that the Samaritan does what the priest and Levite failed to do: he "pours out" the offering of mercy. He also risks his own safety and money by stopping, carrying the man and returning.

p: Two days' wages for a laborer. Enough to keep the man at the inn for some time, and the Samaritan promises more.
b: A denarius was a day's pay for a laborer (Matthew 20:2). Prices for lodging varied, but two denarii would pay for several days' room and board. The promise to cover any extra cost matters: Kenneth Bailey points out that a stranger who could not pay his bill might be held for the debt, and a wounded man with nothing had no protection. The Samaritan, an outsider himself, takes on the whole cost of the man's recovery.

p: The lawyer asked who his neighbor is. Jesus asks who became a neighbor. The neighbor is not someone you qualify but someone you become.
b: The lawyer wanted to know whom he was obliged to love (10:29). Jesus' question asks who acted as a neighbor to the man in need. The answer forces the lawyer to call the Samaritan his model, though he avoids saying the word "Samaritan" (10:37). Many readers since the church fathers have also read the parable as an allegory of salvation, with Christ as the Samaritan (see the chapter page); most modern interpreters read it first as Jesus' answer to the lawyer's question.

p: "Did the mercy with him," a Hebrew-style phrase like doing hesed, loyal love.
b: The Greek phrase poiein eleos meta, "to do mercy with someone," is how the Greek Old Testament renders the Hebrew "to do hesed," loyal love, as in Genesis 24:12 and Ruth 1:8. Mercy here is not a feeling but an act. Jesus' command, "do the same yourself," turns the lawyer's question about eternal life into a call to practice that love. The prophets had already said what God wants: mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6, quoted at Matthew 9:13 as "Mercy is what I want, not sacrifice").
orig: ὁ ποιήσας τὸ ἔλεος μετ' αὐτοῦ (ho poiēsas to eleos met' autou)

p: John places Martha and Mary at Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem. Luke does not name the village, and sets the visit early in the journey.
b: John 11:1 and John 12:1–3 name Bethany, near Jerusalem, as the home of Martha, Mary and their brother Lazarus, and John 12:2 also shows Martha serving. Luke never mentions Lazarus of Bethany and places the visit while Jesus is still far from Jerusalem (13:22; 17:11). Many scholars think Luke arranges his journey section by theme rather than by map; others think he did not know where the sisters lived. Either way the two Gospels agree on the sisters' characters.

a: took him in as her guest
p: Martha receives Jesus as head of the household. Women who hosted the church in their homes appear throughout Acts.
b: The verb hypodechomai means to receive someone as a guest, as Zacchaeus receives Jesus (19:6). Luke names no husband or brother here; Martha (Aramaic for "lady, mistress") seems to be the householder. After the meal at her house, Luke's readers knew women who hosted churches: Mary the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12), Lydia (Acts 16:15) and Nympha (Colossians 4:15). In this chapter about hospitality (9:53; 10:5–8; 10:34–35), Martha does what the Samaritan village refused to do.

p: The posture of a disciple. Mary takes a place usually kept for men who were learning the law.
b: Paul says, "I sat at the feet of Gamaliel" (Acts 22:3), and the Mishnah urges, "sit in the dust of their feet" (Mishnah Avot 1:4), meaning the feet of the sages. To sit at a teacher's feet was to be his student. Jewish sources disagree about teaching women the Torah: Rabbi Eliezer opposed it, Ben Azzai thought a father should teach his daughter (Mishnah Sotah 3:4). Some interpreters say Jesus broke with custom by teaching a woman; Amy-Jill Levine and others warn that this contrast can rest on a stereotype of Judaism, since women did study and teach in some Jewish circles. Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza reads the scene the other way: Luke praises a silent, listening Mary over Martha's active service, which may reflect a church that was limiting women's roles.

p: The word for Martha's serving became the word for ministry, and for deacons.
b: Diakonia and diakoneō are ordinary words for waiting at table. In Luke-Acts they also mean ministry: Jesus says he is among his disciples "as one who serves" (22:27), Judas had a share in the apostles' diakonia (Acts 1:17), and the apostles hand over "serving tables" to the Seven so they can keep to the diakonia of the word (Acts 6:1–4). The women of 8:3 also served Jesus and the Twelve from their own means. So Martha's work is not small. The problem Jesus names is not her serving but her distraction and anxiety (10:41).

a: does it not matter to you
p: Martha uses the words the disciples used in the storm in Mark. Luke left them out there and puts them here.
b: In Mark 4:38 the disciples wake Jesus in the sinking boat: "Teacher, don't you care that we are perishing?" The Greek ou melei soi is the same as Martha's. Luke's account of the storm softens it (8:24), but here a friend speaks to Jesus with the same frankness. Jesus does not rebuke her for asking.

p: In the Bible God or Jesus repeats a name to speak tenderly but firmly.
b: God calls "Abraham, Abraham" at the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:11), "Moses, Moses" at the bush (Exodus 3:4) and "Samuel, Samuel" in the night (1 Samuel 3:10). In Luke Jesus says "Simon, Simon" before warning Peter (22:31), and in Acts the risen Lord calls "Saul, Saul" (Acts 9:4). The doubled name signals affection and an important word to come.

p: Merimnaō: the anxiety that chokes the word in the parable of the sower and that Jesus tells his disciples to drop.
b: In the parable of the sower, the seed among thorns is choked by worries, riches and pleasures (8:14). Jesus will soon tell his disciples not to worry about their lives (12:22–31) but to seek God's kingdom first. Martha is not condemned; she is shown the same choice: the many things, or the one.

p: Meris: a portion, a share. In the Psalms God himself is the believer's portion.
b: Meris is a share of food at a meal, or a share of an inheritance. The psalmist says, "The LORD is the share I was given, and my cup" (Psalm 16:5), and "my share, is God forever" (Psalm 73:26); the Levites had no land because the LORD was their share (Numbers 18:20). Martha is preparing many dishes; Mary has chosen the one portion that matters, the Lord's word, and Jesus says it will not be taken from her. Luke's "good" can mean "best" in this setting, but the Greek says "good."
